claims.feature: ordinary language for hobbit viewpoint vs archaic omniscient passages
claims.claim: Hobbits' points of view are recorded in ordinary language, while other passages use an archaic diction reminiscent of ancient epic and Macpherson's Ossian and convey an omniscient point of view tied to 'epic characters' like Aragorn.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, 'Points of View' (ch. 4) abstract, Springer

claims.claim: Tolkien's limited point of view follows nineteenth-century novelistic practice; Kullmann traces the technique from Walpole's Castle of Otranto (1764) through Pride and Prejudice, Waverley, The Mill on the Floss, Tess, Mary Webb and Buchan's Witch Wood (p. 92).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: Emphasis is laid on subjective experience rather than facts

claims.claim: Like Scott's Waverley and Buchan's David Sempill, the hobbits act as intermediaries and, in Turner's phrase quoted by Kullmann, as representatives of the normality of the reader in a strange environment (pp. 95, 123).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside

claims.feature: mediation as the function of limited POV
claims.claim: The function of the point-of-view technique is mediation: a strange environment and chain of events is brought close to the reader through the intermediate agency of characters whose point of view is recorded; the technique goes back to historical fiction (p. 119).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: brought close to the reader through the intermediate agency

claims.claim: The narrator does not explain why an event has occurred; explanation is left to other characters such as Gandalf or Aragorn, or to the hobbits' own subjective conclusions (p. 91).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: left to other characters, such as Gandalf or Aragorn

claims.claim: Psychonarration (Lanser's term) is reserved to Frodo; what Gandalf thinks or plans is left to Frodo's and the reader's speculation (p. 105).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside

claims.claim: Gandalf speaks a lot but his thoughts and feelings are hardly ever communicated to the reader in third-person narration (p. 118).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: hardly ever communicated to the reader

claims.claim: When Aragorn's viewpoint is used we are told what he sees but learn little of his thoughts and feelings (p. 114); an omniscient passage gives way to a hobbit-limited one to lend Aragorn psychological depth via Merry's gaze (p. 102).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: we do not learn much about his thoughts and feelings

claims.claim: The narrative function of Merry and Pippin is to let the novelist take a hobbit's point of view on each spreading strand of the plot after Frodo and Sam leave the Company at the end of Book 2 (p. 99).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: a hobbit's point of view to each of the spreading strands

claims.feature: focaliser shift from Frodo to Sam
claims.claim: In the first two books Frodo observes the world; later Frodo becomes the object of Sam's gaze, with Sam the focalizer in Books 4 and 6 (pp. 108, 119).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside

claims.feature: limited POV raises tension and characterises
claims.claim: As in nineteenth-century novels, the limited point of view both characterises a person and raises tension; Frodo's viewpoint conveys what he is barely conscious of, e.g. 'finding' he has put on the Ring (p. 105).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside

claims.claim: Sections told by an omniscient narrator are comparatively few, and some (the Prologue, the accounts of Bree and Minas Tirith) resemble a different text type, eighteenth-century antiquarianism such as Percy's Reliques (p. 111).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside

claims.claim: The 'epic style' first seen with the Riders of Rohan recurs particularly at moments when a battle's outcome is imminent: Helm's Deep, the siege of Gondor, and when the Ring falls into the Cracks of Doom (p. 113).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: at moments when the outcome of a battle is imminent

claims.claim: The epic passages' short sentences, parataxis, inversion and repetition, with darkness and night motifs, are reminiscent of Macpherson's Poems of Ossian (p. 116).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: short sentences, parataxis, inversion and repetition

claims.claim: In the Rohirrim passages sentences follow one another paratactically, more complex propositions are built with participles, there are few hypotactic sentences, and the effort of the journey is conveyed by inversions (p. 115).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside

verdicts.note: Raw link.springer.com chapter page reached with a real browser (curl got a 'Client Challenge'; no Wayback capture; Crossref/OpenAlex/S2 abstracts elided). Abstract verbatim: 'While the hobbits’ points of view are recorded in “ordinary” language, other passages are characterised by an archaic diction, reminiscent of ancient epic poetry as well as Macpherson’s Ossian. They convey an omniscient point of view, usually in connection with “epic characters” like Aragorn.' Every limb present. Independently corroborated by the colab.ws Crossref mirror carrying the same abstract.

verdicts.trueWording: Emphasis is laid on subjective experience rather than facts
verdicts.note: Google Books search-inside p.92 verbatim: '… Pride and Prejudice, Waverley, The Mill on the Floss and Tess of the d’Urbervilles; and continued by early twentieth-century novels, such as Mary Webb, Gone to Earth (1917), and John Buchan, Witch Wood (1926). Emphasis is laid on subjective experience rather than facts. One of the earliest examples of this point-of-view technique is certainly Horace Walpole’s The Castle of Otranto: A Gothic Story (1764)…'. Nineteenth-century-practice limb: Springer abstract 'Tolkien follows nineteenth-century novelistic practice' and p.95 'limited point of view (and thus a characteristic feature of nineteenth-century “realist” writing)'; Springer endnote 9 'from Walpole’s Castle of Otranto onwards'. Ordering nuance only: the page lists the novels first, then names Walpole as one of the earliest examples.

Google Books p.95 verbatim: 'Edward Waverley and David Sempill, Tolkien’s hobbits act as intermediaries.' (Sempill introduced p.94 as Buchan’s parish minister, 'the reader’s representative in a strange and exotic environment'; Waverley is Scott’s, p.93). Turner limb confirmed on the raw Springer page, endnote 10 (= p.123): 'A comparison between Scott’s Edward Waverley and Tolkien’s hobbits as focalizers is also established by Turner. Like Waverley in the Scottish highlands, Tolkien’s hobbits act as “representative[s] of the normality of the reader” and “take the role of inexperienced strangers in a big wide, unknown world” (Turner, “One Pair of Eyes,” 24, 22).'

verdicts.trueWording: brought close to the reader through the intermediate agency
verdicts.note: Google Books p.119 verbatim: '… mediation: a strange environment and chain of events is brought close to the reader through the intermediate agency of characters whose point of view is recorded. This technique apparently goes back to historical fiction, as can be seen by looking at Scott’s Waverley and Buchan’s Witch Wood.' All three limbs (mediation, strange environment/chain of events, historical-fiction ancestry) on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: left to other characters, such as Gandalf or Aragorn
verdicts.note: Google Books p.91 verbatim: '… why an event has occurred; this will be left to other characters, such as Gandalf or Aragorn, or to the hobbits’ own subjective conclusions.' Both limbs (narrator withholds the why; explanation devolved to Gandalf/Aragorn or the hobbits’ own conclusions) present.

Google Books p.105 verbatim: 'Psychonarration is reserved to Frodo; what we learn about Gandalf is left open to his, and the reader’s speculation. Neither Frodo nor the reader know about Gandalf’s mind or Gandalf’s plans…'. Lanser attribution confirmed at p.93, where the term is introduced as '“psychonarration” (Lanser, 188)'; Lanser, The Narrative Act, is in the chapter’s Works Cited on the raw Springer page.

verdicts.trueWording: hardly ever communicated to the reader
verdicts.note: Google Books p.118 verbatim: '… he speaks a lot and easily converses with both the hobbits and the “heroes”, his thoughts and feelings are hardly ever communicated to the reader in the form of third-person narration. He obviously needs to remain enigmatic…'. Subject is Gandalf: p.105 makes Gandalf the withheld mind, and Springer endnote 31 says 'We only know about Gandalf’s feelings from what he speaks, so we do not know what he really thinks…'.

verdicts.trueWording: we do not learn much about his thoughts and feelings
verdicts.note: Both limbs on the page. p.113: 'Aragorn’s point of view is usually confined to factual perceptions'; p.114 verbatim: '… we do not learn much about his thoughts and feelings.' p.102 verbatim: 'an omniscient point of view gives way to a passage limited to the point of view of the hobbit. This obviously enables the narrator to lend greater psychological depth to Aragorn’s appearance than to that of the other warriors. At the same time, we (as readers) can only guess at what really passes in Aragorn’s mind; our position is that of Merry, our representative in the story.'

verdicts.trueWording: a hobbit's point of view to each of the spreading strands
verdicts.note: Google Books p.99 verbatim: 'narrative function of Merry and Pippin, however, seems to consist in allowing the novelist to take a hobbit’s point of view to each of the spreading strands of the narrative. After Frodo and Sam leave the Company at the end of book 2 to set out to Mordor on their own, Pippin and Merry are captured by Orcs.' Page says 'strands of the narrative' where the claim paraphrases 'strand of the plot' — the quoted string itself is verbatim.

Google Books p.108 verbatim: 'In the first two books, it was Frodo who observed and experienced the world around him. Now it is Frodo who is looked at from an outside point of view, as he becomes the object of Sam’s gaze. Frodo’s gradual fading away as a focalizer…'. Books 4 and 6 limb confirmed at p.119: '… focalizer in books 4 and 6.'

verdicts.trueWording: he found that he had put it back in his pocket
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the example — 'finding' he has put ON the Ring; pp.104–105 give the opposite action, Frodo finding he had put the Ring back in his POCKET instead of casting it into the fire (LotR 60)
verdicts.note: Claim carries no quote field, so no verbatim match was possible. Supported limbs, verbatim at p.105: 'Frodo’s point of view thus serves to convey information about his mind of which Frodo himself is barely conscious. As in nineteenth-century novels, the limited point of view can both characterize a person and raise tension with regard to the story.' The unsupported limb is the illustration: p.104 quotes LotR 60 — 'he made a movement, as if to cast it away — but he found that he had put it back in his pocket' — and p.105 glosses 'Frodo “found” that he had done so; this had been an involuntary, almost unconscious action.' Nothing on p.105 has Frodo finding he has put the Ring on.

Google Books p.111 verbatim: '… comparatively few in number, and some of them resemble a different type of text altogether: The “prologue” (1–16) and the accounts of Bree (149–151) and Minas Tirith (751–752)…'. Percy limb also on p.111: '“eighteenth-century antiquarianism”, as found, for example, in the manifold paratexts of Thomas Percy’ Reliques of Ancient English Poetry (1765) (Groom 291–296)' (cross-referenced from p.34 n.43, '“eighteenth-century antiquarianism” found in these texts, see below, Chap. 4'). Note for completeness: the same page also likens those passages to 'ethnographic accounts or even of travel guides' and to ancient Greek romance — the claim reports only the antiquarianism comparandum, but every limb it does assert is on the page.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'first seen with the Riders of Rohan' — pp.112–113 place the style's first appearance in a Rivendell passage ('The Sword of Elendil was forged anew by Elvish smiths…', LotR 276–277), contrasted with 'the previous accounts of the proceedings in the house of Elrond'; the Riders of Rohan are not reached until p.115
verdicts.note: The quotation itself is verbatim at p.113: '… will recur several times, particularly at moments when the outcome of a battle is imminent, as at Helm’s Deep (541), at the siege of Gondor (817) and when the Ring falls into the Cracks of Doom (948).' All three battle-crisis instances check out. Only the origin attribution fails: p.113 says the '“epic style” which first appears here' — 'here' being the p.112 Sword-of-Elendil passage — and adds that it will also be used where no hobbit is present, 'as in large parts of book 3'.

verdicts.trueWording: short sentences, parataxis, inversion and repetition
verdicts.note: Google Books p.116 verbatim: '… short sentences, parataxis, inver-sion and repetition, as well as motifs concerning darkness and night-time, are reminiscent of Macpherson’s Poems of Ossian, as in a passage in which Fingal, the hero, approaches his enemies…'. The only departures from the claim's quote are the printed line-break hyphens in 'inver- sion' and 'night- time'. Darkness/night-motif limb present in the same sentence; Macpherson's debt also noted in Springer endnote 29 (Groom 295).

Google Books p.115 verbatim: '… paratactically. More complex propositions are constructed by means of participles, while there are few hypotactical sentences. The effort involved in the journey is conveyed by means of inversions (“swift and enduring”, “forty leagues or more”) and repetition (“many leagues”, “forty leagues”).' All four limbs present. Rohirrim context confirmed on the same and next page: p.115 'Riders of Rohan, as in the passage which depicts their setting off from Edoras to the battle of Helm’s Deep'; p.116 'The account of the riding is limited to the bare facts… the archaic language and sentence construction characterizes the Riders as epical warriors'.
